mainTopic: Repetitions in the משנה about רגל and שן, the מחלוקת over pebbles (צרורות), and when indirect damage counts as the animal's body
overview: The גמרא first asks why our משנה seems to repeat itself, saying both 'the foot is מועדת' and 'the animal is מועדת'. רבא answers that the first line teaches the main category (אב) and the second teaches its offshoots (תולדות). רב אשי explains a similar repetition in the eating section: one line is about a חיה and the other about a בהמה. The גמרא then discusses why the משנה lists its cases in this order. Next, a ברייתא lists all the ways a walking animal causes full damage. סומכוס holds that pebbles (צרורות) kicked up by an animal also pay full damage, while the רבנן say half, and several ברייתות about chickens show the same מחלוקת. רבא explains that the רבנן agree an animal's force is like its body, but the half payment for pebbles is a הלכה learned by tradition. He also compares damages to the laws of a זב, which teaches that a cart pulled by a calf counts as the animal's body. Finally, רבא asks whether a vessel that an animal stepped on, and that rolled away and broke, counts as body damage or as pebbles. The גמרא's attempts to answer this continue onto the next amud.

steps.title: Why does the משנה say 'foot' and 'animal' twice?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רבא why the משנה mentions both the רגל and the בהמה for the same walking damage. They seem to be the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רבינא said to רבא: 'The foot' is the same as 'the animal'! Why say it twice?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by pointing out what looks like a repetition in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the walking-damage section, the משנה says the רגל is מועדת to break things as it walks. It then also says the בהמה is מועדת to walk normally and break things. Damage done while walking is the same idea both times, so רבינא asks what the second line adds.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion section that analyzes the משנה
Foot; the category of damage done by an animal while walking

phrases.english: GEMARA: Ravina said to Rava:
Foot is the same as animal!
phrases.notes: The משנה says both 'the foot is מועדת' and 'the animal is מועדת' about walking damage, which sounds like saying the same thing twice.

steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the משנה listing both רגל and בהמה as מועדת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two lines that describe the same walking damage look redundant.

steps.title: First the main category, then its offshoots
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the משנה first teaches the אבות (main categories) and then the תולדות (subcategories).
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The תנא first taught the main categories, and then he teaches the subcategories.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains that the two lines are not repetitive. Each one teaches a different level of the law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The foot' is the main category of רגל, which the Torah itself mentions. 'The animal' covers the offshoots: damage done by other parts of the body while the animal walks. So the second line adds new cases.

keyTerms.meaning: The teacher of the משנה; 'he taught'

phrases.english: He said to him: He taught the primary categories,
and then he teaches the subcategories.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the redundancy question
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each line has a different job (main category vs. offshoot)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both lines say the same thing about walking damage
steps.terutzMaskana: Line one is the אב of רגל; line two adds its תולדות

steps.title: The eating section also repeats itself
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges רבא: the later section about שן also says both 'the tooth is מועדת' and 'the animal is מועדת'. There are no offshoots there.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, the later clause says 'the tooth is מועדת' and 'the animal is מועדת'. What main categories and subcategories are there?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks רבא's answer by pointing to a similar repetition where his answer does not seem to work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If repetition always means 'main category, then offshoots', the eating section should list offshoots too. But that section only talks about eating fruits and vegetables. So רבא's explanation does not cover the whole משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: But now, if so (introducing a challenge to what was just said)
The later clause of the משנה
Tooth; the category of damage done by eating
Forewarned; the owner pays in full because this damage is expected

phrases.english: But now, if so,
the latter clause, which teaches:
"The tooth is forewarned"... "the animal is forewarned,"
phrases.notes: This is the משנה later on (19b) about an animal eating fruits and vegetables.

phrases.english: what primary categories and what subcategories are there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer from step 2
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's answer of אבות and תולדות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same repetition appears in the eating section, where there are no offshoots, so the answer does not hold.

steps.title: רבא's joking reply
steps.stepSummary: רבא jokingly answers: 'I explained one repetition; now you explain the other one.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered him with a joke and said to him: I answered one; you answer one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא does not give a real answer here. He playfully hands the question back to רבינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא admits that his אבות and תולדות idea only works for the walking section. The eating section still needs its own explanation, and he leaves that job to רבינא.

phrases.english: He was replying to him jokingly,
and said to him: I resolved one,
and you resolve one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the challenge without solving it
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No real answer here. רב אשי explains the eating section's repetition in Step 6.

steps.title: So why does the eating section repeat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the real reason behind the repetition in the eating section.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next move. It asks the question that רבא left open, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבא's joke did not solve the problem, the גמרא now looks for a real explanation of why the eating section mentions both שן and בהמה.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the reason? (asks for the logic behind something)

phrases.english: And what is the reason?
phrases.notes: He means: why does the eating section of the משנה say 'מועדת' twice?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the question רבא left unanswered
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the eating section mentions both 'the tooth' and 'the animal' as מועדת

steps.title: Wild animal first, then domestic animal
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the משנה first teaches eating damage by a חיה and then by a בהמה. This teaches that a חיה is included even though the פסוק says 'בעירה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The תנא taught the tooth of a wild animal, and then he teaches the tooth of a domestic animal. You might have thought that since the פסוק says 'And he sends out his animal', only a domestic animal counts and a wild animal does not. So it teaches us that a wild animal is included in 'animal'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives the real answer. The two lines in the eating section are about two different kinds of animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The tooth is מועדת' refers to a חיה, and 'the animal is מועדת' refers to a בהמה. Without the משנה, we might think the word בעירה in the פסוק limits eating damage to domestic animals. The משנה teaches that a חיה is included too, so its owner is also liable.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have thought to say

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the owner of a wild animal is liable for eating damage just like the owner of a domestic animal.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
He taught the tooth of a wild animal,
and then he teaches the tooth of a domestic animal.
It would enter your mind to say:
"And he sends out his animal" is written,
a domestic animal, yes; a wild animal, no;

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּחַיָּה בִּכְלַל בְּהֵמָה.
phrases.english: it teaches us that a wild animal is included in 'animal'.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא שֵׁן דְּחַיָּה וְקָתָנֵי שֵׁן דִּבְהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each line refers to a different type of animal
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word בעירה limits eating damage to domestic animals
steps.terutzMaskana: A חיה is included in eating damage, and the משנה states it separately to teach this

steps.title: Then the domestic animal should come first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the חיה is learned from the בהמה, the משנה should mention the בהמה first.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, he should have taught it first!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the order of the משנה under רב אשי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בהמה is the main case written in the Torah, and the חיה is only included through it. Logically, the main case should be listed before the case that depends on it. Yet the משנה lists the חיה first.

phrases.english: If so,
he should have taught it first!
phrases.notes: He means the domestic animal, the main case, should have been listed first.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי הָא מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְמִיתְנֵי בְּרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the order implied by רב אשי's answer
steps.kashyaTarget: The order of the משנה under רב אשי's reading
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The main case (בהמה) should come before the case derived from it (חיה).

steps.title: A law from a derivation is dear to the תנא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the חיה comes first because a law learned through a דרשה is dear to the תנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: This law, which comes to him from a derivation, is dear to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the order. The תנא chose to lead with the law he worked out himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law about a חיה is not written openly in the פסוק. It comes from a דרשה. Because it took effort to learn, the תנא treasures it and lists it before the obvious case of a בהמה.

keyTerms.meaning: A derivation; a law learned by interpreting a פסוק

steps.whatToRemember: Walking section: 'foot' is the main category and 'animal' adds the offshoots (רבא). Eating section: 'tooth' is a חיה and 'animal' is a בהמה (רב אשי). The חיה comes first because a law from a דרשה is dear to the תנא.

phrases.english: This, which comes to him from a derivation,
is dear to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי דְּאָתְיָא לֵיהּ מִדְּרָשָׁא חֲבִיבָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about the order
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the order by the תנא's preference
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The main case should be listed first
steps.terutzMaskana: A law learned through a דרשה is cherished, so it is listed first

steps.title: Why not put the derived case first in the opening clause too?
steps.stepSummary: If a law learned through a דרשה is dear to the תנא, the opening clause of the משנה should also list the derived case first.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then in the first clause too, the תנא should teach first the case that is not written in the פסוק!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from Step 8. If the תנא likes to put the derived law first, he should have done the same in the משנה's first clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the opening clause, the משנה first says 'the foot is מועדת', which is the אב written in the תורה. Only afterward does it say 'the animal is מועדת', which covers the תולדות: damage by the body, hair and so on, which are not written. By the rule of Step 8, the unwritten case should have come first.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if your reasoning is right
Let him teach; he should have taught

phrases.english: If so, in the first clause too
phrases.notes: The 'first clause' is the משנה's opening: 'the foot is מועדת', and then 'the animal is מועדת' for its body and other parts.

phrases.english: let him teach that case
which is not written, first!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the answer of Step 8 against another clause of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The principle that a law learned through a דרשה is dear to the תנא and so comes first.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Applied consistently, the principle should also put 'the animal is מועדת' (the unwritten תולדות) before 'the foot is מועדת' (the written אב) in the opening clause, but the משנה does not.

steps.title: The two cases are not comparable: a primary category versus a subcategory
steps.stepSummary: With eating, חיה and בהמה are both primary categories, so the derived one can come first. In the walking clause, the בהמה line (body, hair and so on) is only a subcategory, so the תנא would not put it before the primary category of רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? There, both cases are primary categories, so the one learned from a דרשה is dear to him. Here, would he skip the primary category and teach the subcategory first?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the cases are different. The 'dear derived law goes first' rule only works when both cases are on the same level.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage by eating, whether by a חיה or a בהמה, is a full primary category (אב) of שן, so either one may go first. In the walking clause, damage by the animal's body, hair and similar parts is only a תולדה of רגל. Putting a subcategory ahead of its own primary category would be out of order.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? (rejects the comparison)
A subcategory that comes from a primary category

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think damage by the animal's body stops being part of רגל. It is still in the רגל family, but only as a תולדה, which is exactly why it cannot come before the אב.

phrases.english: How can you compare?!
There, both this and that are primary categories,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the eating case: damage by a בהמה and by a חיה.

phrases.aramaic: הָךְ דְּאָתְיָא לֵיהּ מִדְּרָשָׁא – חֲבִיבָא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: so the one that comes to him through a דרשה is dear to him.
Here, would he leave aside the primary category
and teach a subcategory first?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends Step 8 against the challenge of Step 9 by showing the two clauses are different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'dear derived law' rule should apply everywhere in the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule applies only when both cases are primary categories. A תולדה never goes before its אב.

steps.title: Another answer: continuing from the end of the previous פרק
steps.stepSummary: Since the last פרק ended with רגל, the תנא opened this פרק with רגל too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you wish, say: since he finished with the foot, he began with the foot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, simpler reason why the משנה starts with רגל: it continues where the previous פרק left off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last משנה of the first פרק ended with the foot breaking things as it walks. So the תנא picks up the new פרק with that same topic. This explains the order without the אב/תולדה distinction.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (introduces another answer)
Since; because (one thing flows into the next)

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
since he finished with the foot,
phrases.notes: The previous פרק (15b) closed with a line about the foot breaking things as it walks.

phrases.english: he began with the foot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to Step 9, separate from the answer in Step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative explanation based on the order of the משניות
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The order must come from the 'dear derived law' rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The order follows the flow from the end of the previous perek.
steps.whatToRemember: Two reasons the משנה starts with רגל: (1) the בהמה line (body, hair and so on) is only a תולדה and cannot come before its אב; (2) the previous פרק ended with רגל, so this one opens with it.

steps.title: A ברייתא: all the ways a walking animal causes full damage
steps.stepSummary: A walking animal is מועד to break things. Damage with its body, hair, saddle, saddlebag, halter, bell, or a donkey's load pays full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: an animal is considered forewarned to walk in its usual way and break things. How so? If an animal entered the injured person's yard and damaged with its body as it walked, or with its hair as it walked, or with the saddle on it, the saddlebag on it, the halter in its mouth, or the bell on its neck, or a donkey with its load, the owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists the many ways an animal can damage just by walking normally. All of them count as רגל and pay נזק שלם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רגל is not only the actual foot. Anything that is part of the animal or attached to it as it walks normally is treated the same way. That is why all these cases pay full damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Forewarned; expected to do this, so full payment
In the course of its walking

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
An animal is forewarned to walk in its usual way
and to break things. How so?
An animal that entered the injured person's yard
and damaged with its body as it walked,
or with its hair as it walked;
with the saddle on it, or with the saddlebag on it,
or with the halter in its mouth, or with the bell on its neck;
or a donkey with its load
the owner pays full damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בְּהֵמָה מוּעֶדֶת לְהַלֵּךְ כְּדַרְכָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section with a ברייתא about damage done while walking.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Damage done by an animal's body, hair, or attached gear while it walks normally in the injured person's yard pays נזק שלם.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רגל covers more than the hoof: anything that moves with the animal as it walks is treated the same.

steps.title: סומכוס adds pebbles and a burrowing pig
steps.stepSummary: סומכוס says that pebbles kicked up by the animal, and a pig burrowing in a garbage heap that damaged, also pay full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: סומכוס says: pebbles, and a pig that was burrowing in the garbage heap and caused damage: the owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: סומכוס gives his own view inside the ברייתא. He holds that pebbles kicked up by walking, and a pig digging in garbage, also pay full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה rules that pebbles pay only half damage, so סומכוס is disagreeing with it. For him, pebbles count as full רגל damage. The wording about the pig is unclear, and the next step questions it.

keyTerms.meaning: Pebbles kicked up by the animal as it walks

phrases.english: סומכוס says: pebbles,
and a pig that was burrowing in the garbage heap and caused damage
the owner pays full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with סומכוס's added cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to סומכוס, pebbles kicked up by an animal, and a pig burrowing in garbage that causes damage, pay נזק שלם.

steps.title: If the pig caused damage, that is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what סומכוס adds by saying a pig that damaged pays full. That seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'It caused damage' — that is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of סומכוס. Of course a pig that directly damages while burrowing pays full, so what is the new point?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Burrowing is a pig's normal way of moving about, so direct damage from it is plain רגל. Saying it pays full teaches nothing new, which suggests the wording needs fixing.

phrases.english: 'It caused damage' — that is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of סומכוס in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: סומכוס's statement about the pig that burrowed and caused damage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Direct damage from normal burrowing is obviously full damage, so the statement seems to teach nothing.

steps.title: Correct the wording: the pig kicked up pebbles
steps.stepSummary: Read סומכוס as saying the pig kicked up pebbles that caused damage, and still the owner pays full.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: it kicked up pebbles and caused damage — the owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording. The pig did not damage directly; it sprayed pebbles while burrowing, and סומכוס still requires full payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the line teaches something new. Even indirect damage through pebbles kicked up by a burrowing pig pays full, which fits סומכוס's general view on צרורות.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
it kicked up pebbles and caused damage
the owner pays full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 14 by correcting the wording of סומכוס.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the reading of the text
steps.terutzHavaAmina: סומכוס was talking about a pig that damaged directly, which would be obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: סומכוס means a pig that sprayed pebbles while burrowing; even that pays נזק שלם.
steps.whatToRemember: For סומכוס, pebbles kicked up by an animal, even by a pig digging in garbage, pay full damage, not half.

steps.title: Who mentioned pebbles at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why סומכוס speaks about pebbles when the earlier part of the ברייתא never mentioned them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pebbles — who said anything about them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a gap. סומכוס argues about pebbles, but the first part of the ברייתא never talked about pebbles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סומכוס says pebbles pay full damage, which sounds like he is disagreeing with someone who said less. But the first opinion in the ברייתא only listed body, hair, saddle and similar items, and never mentioned pebbles. So who is סומכוס arguing with?

keyTerms.meaning: Pebbles kicked up by an animal while walking, which cause damage indirectly
Who mentioned them? A standard way to ask why a topic suddenly appears

phrases.english: Pebbles — who mentioned their name?
phrases.notes: The first part of the ברייתא (step 12) never spoke about pebbles, so it is strange that סומכוס argues about them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 15 explained סומכוס's words, the גמרא now notices that his topic, pebbles, has no earlier opinion to argue against.
steps.kashyaTarget: The structure of the ברייתא, where סומכוס seems to argue about a case nobody mentioned
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An argument needs a first opinion. Since the תנא קמא never mentioned pebbles, סומכוס's ruling about pebbles has no one to disagree with.

steps.title: The ברייתא is missing words: pebbles pay half
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is missing a line. The first opinion says pebbles and a pig kicking up pebbles pay half damage, and סומכוס says full damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא is missing words, and this is what it teaches: pebbles kicked up in the normal way pay half damage. A pig burrowing in a garbage heap that kicked up pebbles and damaged pays half damage. סומכוס says: pebbles, and a pig burrowing in a garbage heap that kicked up pebbles and damaged, pay full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that some words are missing from the ברייתא and fills them in. The first opinion says pebbles pay half damage, and סומכוס disagrees and says full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the missing line added, there is now a real argument. The תנא קמא holds that pebbles kicked up in the animal's normal way pay only חצי נזק, and this includes the pig's pebbles. סומכוס says that in both cases the owner pays נזק שלם.

keyTerms.meaning: The text is missing words, so the גמרא fills them in
In their normal way, meaning the animal kicked up pebbles while walking normally
Half the cost of the damage
And it sent something flying, here pebbles

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the חצי נזק of a שור תם that gores. Here the animal is acting normally, and the half payment for pebbles is a separate rule.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main מחלוקת of the סוגיא: does damage from an animal's indirect force (צרורות) pay half, like the רבנן say, or full, like סומכוס says?

phrases.english: It is missing words,
and this is what it teaches:
Pebbles kicked up in their normal way — half damage.
phrases.notes: This is the missing line. It gives the first opinion that סומכוס will argue with.

phrases.english: And a pig that was burrowing in a garbage heap,
and sent pebbles flying and damaged — pays half damage.
סומכוס says: pebbles,
and a pig that was burrowing in a garbage heap
and sent pebbles flying and damaged — pays full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by adding the missing first opinion about pebbles.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Filling in missing words in the ברייתא (חסורי מחסרא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא as written has no first opinion about pebbles, so סומכוס seems to argue with no one.
steps.terutzMaskana: The full ברייתא has the תנא קמא saying pebbles pay חצי נזק, and סומכוס says נזק שלם.

steps.title: Chickens flying: wings pay full, wind pays half
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: chickens that broke vessels with their wings pay full damage. If the wind from their wings broke them, the owner pays half, and סומכוס says full.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: chickens that were flying from place to place and broke vessels with their wings, the owner pays full damage. If they broke them with the wind of their wings, he pays half damage. סומכוס says: full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with the same argument, now about chickens. When the wing itself breaks something it is full damage, but when only the wind from the wing breaks it, the רבנן say half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wing hitting the vessel is the animal's own body, so it pays full. The wind is only a force that the animal created, like pebbles, so the רבנן say חצי נזק. סומכוס stays consistent and says נזק שלם.

keyTerms.meaning: With the wind from their wings

phrases.english: The רבנן taught: chickens that were flying
from place to place, and broke vessels with their wings —
he pays full damage.
With the wind of their wings — they pay half damage.
סומכוס says: full damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: תַּרְנְגוֹלִין שֶׁהָיוּ מַפְרִיחִין מִמָּקוֹם לְמָקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the same pebbles argument between the רבנן and סומכוס in a new case, the wind from chickens' wings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The animal's own body, its wings, pays full. Wind from the wings pays half according to the רבנן and full according to סומכוס.

steps.title: Chickens hopping on dough: pecking pays full, kicked-up dirt pays half
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא: chickens hopping on dough or fruit that dirtied or pecked it pay full. If they kicked up dirt or pebbles, the owner pays half, and סומכוס says full.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: chickens that were hopping on dough or on fruit and dirtied it or pecked at it, the owner pays full damage. If they kicked up dirt or pebbles, he pays half damage. סומכוס says: full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא with the same pattern. Direct damage pays full, and dirt or pebbles kicked up pay half according to the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dirtying the food with their feet or pecking it is direct damage by the body, so it pays full. Dirt and pebbles kicked up are צרורות, so the רבנן say half. סומכוס again says full.

phrases.english: Another ברייתא teaches:
Chickens that were hopping

phrases.aramaic: עַל גַּבֵּי עִיסָּה וְעַל גַּבֵּי פֵּירוֹת,
phrases.english: on top of dough and on top of fruit,

phrases.aramaic: וְטִינְּפוּ אוֹ נִיקְּרוּ – מְשַׁלֵּם נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם.
phrases.english: and dirtied it or pecked it — he pays full damage.

phrases.aramaic: הֶעֱלוּ עָפָר אוֹ צְרוֹרוֹת – מְשַׁלְּמִין חֲצִי נֶזֶק.
phrases.english: If they kicked up dirt or pebbles — they pay half damage.
סומכוס says: full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second chicken case showing the same argument between the רבנן and סומכוס.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Dirtying or pecking pays full. Kicked-up dirt or pebbles pay half according to the רבנן and full according to סומכוס.

steps.title: An unnamed ברייתא: wind from a chicken's wings pays half
steps.stepSummary: A third ברייתא says without any argument that wind from under a flying chicken's wings that broke vessels pays half damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: a chicken that was flying from place to place, and wind came out from under its wings and broke the vessels, the owner pays half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that rules half damage for wind from wings, and it names no one who disagrees. This sets up the next line, which tells us whose view it follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same case as the wind in step 18. Here, though, the ruling of חצי נזק is given as a plain rule, with no mention of סומכוס.

phrases.english: Another ברייתא teaches:
A chicken that was flying from place to place,
and wind came out from under its wings

phrases.aramaic: וְשִׁיבְּרָה אֶת הַכֵּלִים – מְשַׁלֵּם חֲצִי נֶזֶק.
phrases.english: and broke the vessels — he pays half damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: תַּרְנְגוֹל שֶׁהָיָה מַפְרִיחַ מִמָּקוֹם לְמָקוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the wind case from step 18 as an unnamed ruling with no argument.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wind from under a flying chicken's wings that breaks vessels pays חצי נזק.

steps.title: The unnamed ברייתא follows the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that this unnamed ברייתא follows the רבנן, not סומכוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: This unnamed ruling follows the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us that the unnamed ברייתא from step 20 agrees with the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סומכוס would require full damage for wind, so a ruling of half can only follow the רבנן. This short note identifies whose opinion the ברייתא follows.

keyTerms.meaning: An unnamed ruling, with no author mentioned
Following the opinion of the רבנן

phrases.english: The unnamed ruling follows the רבנן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the author of the ברייתא in step 20.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ruling of חצי נזק for wind from wings is the opinion of the רבנן.

steps.title: רבא: Why do the רבנן say half?
steps.stepSummary: רבא understands סומכוס, who holds that an animal's force is like its body. But the רבנן are hard to understand: if force is like the body, the owner should pay full, and if not, he should pay nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: סומכוס makes sense, because he holds that an animal's force counts like its body. But the רבנן: if force counts like the body, the owner should pay full damage. And if it does not count like the body, he should not even pay half damage!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא challenges the רבנן's opinion of half damage. Half seems to fit neither possibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא lays out only two options. Either force is like the body, which means full payment, or it is not, which means no payment for רגל at all. Half damage seems to make no sense under either option.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense. This introduces the side that is easy before the difficult side
His force is like his body, meaning damage by an animal's force counts as if its body did it
If ... and if. The גמרא sets out two options

steps.whatToRemember: סומכוס: כחו כגופו, so the owner pays full for צרורות. The רבנן say half, and רבא asks how half can fit either option.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not questioning the ברייתות themselves. He accepts that the רבנן say half. He is asking for the reasoning behind it.

phrases.english: רבא said: It makes sense for סומכוס —
he holds: its force is like its body.
But the רבנן — if it is like its body —
he should have to pay all the damage;
and if it is not like its body,
he should not pay even half damage!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתות show the argument, רבא questions the reasoning behind the רבנן's half payment.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's ruling that צרורות pay חצי נזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A two-sided question: if force is like the body, the owner pays full; if not, he pays nothing. Half fits neither side.

steps.title: רבא: Force Is Like the Body, but Pebbles Are a Special Tradition
steps.stepSummary: רבא retracts and explains that the רבנן agree force is like the body. The half payment for צרורות is a הלכה they received by tradition.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then רבא said: Really, force is like the animal's body. The half payment for pebbles is a הלכה that was learned by tradition.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his own question from the last step. He says the רבנן also hold that force counts as the body, but pebbles get half payment because of a special tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 22, the רבנן seemed illogical: they should require either full payment or nothing. Now רבא explains that by plain logic they would require full payment. The half payment is not built on reasoning; it is a fixed rule passed down by tradition (הלכה למשה מסיני), and that removes the contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: He went back (he changed his mind)
It is like its body (the force counts as the animal itself)
They learned it as a הלכה by tradition

steps.whatToRemember: According to the רבנן, force is really like the body. Half damage for צרורות is a special הלכה from tradition, not something worked out by logic.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the base for the famous rule that the half payment for צרורות is a הלכה received by tradition.

phrases.english: Then Rava said:
Actually, it is like its body,
and half damage for pebbles —
they learned it as a halacha by tradition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא רבא raised against the רבנן in step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The rule rests on tradition rather than reasoning
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן's half payment seemed to fit neither 'force is like the body' nor 'force is not like the body.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן hold force is like the body. The half payment for pebbles is a separate tradition.

steps.title: רבא's Rule: Damages Follow the Laws of a זב
steps.stepSummary: רבא teaches that any kind of contact that makes a vessel טמא when a זב does it brings full payment in damages. Any contact that leaves it טהור brings half payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Whatever a זב makes impure, an animal doing the same thing pays full damage. Whatever a זב leaves pure, an animal doing the same thing pays half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new general rule. He uses the laws of how a זב makes things impure as a guide for when an animal's owner pays full or half damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some contact with a זב counts as his own touch and makes a vessel טמא. Other contact is too indirect and leaves it טהור. רבא says damages work the same way: 'direct' contact means full payment, and 'indirect' contact means half payment.

keyTerms.meaning: A man with a certain discharge whose contact can make things impure

phrases.english: Rava said:
Anything that, with a zav, is impure —
phrases.notes: He means any kind of contact that, if a זב did it to a vessel, would make the vessel impure.

phrases.english: in damages, he pays full damage.
Anything that, with a zav, is pure —
in damages, he pays half damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement by רבא about the same topic of direct and indirect damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Contact that makes a vessel טמא with a זב brings full payment; contact that leaves it טהור brings half payment.

steps.title: Did רבא Only Come to Teach the Pebbles Law?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא needed to say this. Half payment for indirect damage is already known from צרורות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And did רבא come to teach us the law of pebbles?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's rule. The half-payment part seems to teach nothing new, since we already know pebbles pay half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתות in steps 17-20 already taught that indirect damage, like kicked-up pebbles, pays half. If רבא's rule only taught that, it would be repeating a known law. So the גמרא asks what new point he is making.

keyTerms.meaning: Pebbles (damage done by things the animal kicks up)

phrases.english: And Rava — did he come to teach us pebbles?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's rule from step 24 as adding nothing new.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Half payment for indirect damage is already known from the law of צרורות, so the rule seems unnecessary.

steps.title: רבא Teaches the Case of a Calf Pulling a Cart
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא's new point is a calf pulling a cart. Damage done by the cart counts as the animal's own body, so the owner pays in full.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. רבא is teaching us about a calf pulling a cart.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבא's rule is not about pebbles; it teaches the new case of a cart pulled by a calf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vessel that a זב moves is treated as though he touched it. In the same way, a cart pulled by an animal is treated like the animal's body, so its damage is full payment and not like pebbles. This is the new law that comes out of רבא's comparison to a זב.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he teaches us

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the cart is like pebbles just because the calf does not touch the object directly. רבא's whole point is that the cart counts as the animal's body, so the owner pays full damage.

phrases.english: No; Rava —
a calf pulling a cart —
this is what he teaches us.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא; רָבָא – עֶגְלָה מוֹשֶׁכֶת בַּקָּרוֹן קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 25 by naming the new case רבא is teaching.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the new case the statement teaches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's rule seemed to repeat the law of צרורות.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא's rule teaches that damage from a cart pulled by a calf counts as body damage and brings full payment.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that something attached to and moved along by the animal counts like the animal itself.

steps.title: A ברייתא Supports רבא: Full Payment for a Calf Pulling a Cart
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists damage done while walking: by the animal's body, its hair, its gear, a donkey's load, or a calf pulling a cart. In all these cases the owner pays full damage, just as רבא said.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא supports רבא: An animal is מועדת to break things as it walks. If it entered the injured person's yard and damaged with its body, hair, saddle, saddlebag, halter, or bell, or a donkey with its load, or a calf pulling a cart, the owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that agrees with רבא. It includes a calf pulling a cart among the cases where the owner pays full damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא treats everything attached to the animal (gear, load, cart) like the animal's own body. A calf pulling a cart is listed outright as full payment. That is exactly the new point רבא made in step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught that agrees with him
Forewarned, known to do this, so the owner pays in full

steps.whatToRemember: Damage done while walking by the animal's body, or by anything attached to it, including a cart it pulls, brings full payment. This supports רבא.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita in accordance with Rava:
An animal is forewarned to break things
in the course of its walking. How so?
An animal that entered the yard of the injured person —
and it did damage with its body as it walked,
or with its hair as it walked;
with the saddle on it, or with the saddlebag on it,
or with the halter in its mouth, or with the bell on its neck;
or a donkey with its load, or a calf pulling a cart —
phrases.notes: This is the line that backs up רבא's case from step 26.

phrases.english: he pays full damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא supporting רבא's case of the calf and cart from step 26.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's ruling that damage from a cart pulled by a calf brings full payment
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing a calf pulling a cart among the cases of full payment

steps.title: Chickens peck through a bucket rope and the owner pays in full
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if chickens peck through a bucket's rope and the bucket falls and breaks, the owner pays נזק שלם.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: chickens were pecking at the rope of a bucket. The rope snapped and the bucket broke. The owner pays full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא. It shows a case where damage happens through something connected to the animal's action, and the owner still pays in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chickens never touched the bucket itself. They only cut the rope, and the bucket broke when it fell. Still, the ברייתא treats it as the chickens' own direct damage, so it is נזק שלם and not the half payment of צרורות.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Chickens that were pecking
at the rope of a bucket,
and the rope snapped and the bucket broke,
they pay full damage.
phrases.notes: "They" means the owners of the chickens.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: תַּרְנְגוֹלִים שֶׁהָיוּ מְחַטְּטִין בְּחֶבֶל דְּלִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another ברייתא in the same direction as Step 27. Damage done through something connected to the animal counts as its body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Chickens that peck through a bucket's rope and cause the bucket to break: the owner pays נזק שלם.

steps.title: An animal steps on a vessel that later rolls away and breaks
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether a vessel stepped on by an animal, which then rolls away and breaks, counts as the animal's body (full payment) or as צרורות (half payment).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: an animal stepped on a vessel but did not break it. The vessel rolled to another place and broke there. What is the law? Do we follow the beginning, so it counts as the animal's own body? Or do we follow the place where the vessel broke, so it counts like pebbles?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a question he does not know the answer to. Which moment decides how the owner pays: the animal's first push, or the actual breaking?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we look at the start, the animal touched the vessel directly. That is its גופו and brings נזק שלם. If we look at the moment of breaking, the vessel broke later and away from the animal, just like צרורות. That would bring only חצי נזק.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question he does not know the answer to
We follow the beginning of the action
Pebbles kicked up by an animal; a case of indirect damage with half payment

phrases.english: Rava asked:
It stepped on a vessel and did not break it,
and the vessel rolled to another place and broke,
what is the law?
Do we follow the beginning,
so it is its body,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא בָּתַר תְּבַר מָנָא אָזְלִינָא –
phrases.english: or perhaps we follow the breaking of the vessel,
so it counts like pebbles?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the clear cases of full payment, רבא asks about a borderline case where the touch was direct but the breaking was indirect.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does liability follow the first act (the animal's body, full payment) or the final breaking (צרורות, half payment)?
steps.whyThisMatters: The question turns on a basic idea in נזיקין: which moment decides what kind of damage it is.

steps.title: Trying to answer from רבה's case of a vessel thrown off a roof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests solving רבא's question from רבה. Someone who smashes a vessel already falling from a roof is פטור, because the vessel counts as already broken. This seems to show that we follow the beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: Answer it from רבה. רבה said: someone threw a vessel off the top of a roof, and another person came and broke it with a stick on the way down. The second person is exempt, because we tell him: you broke a broken vessel!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer רבא's question with a ruling of רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה treats the vessel as broken from the moment it was thrown, even though it had not shattered yet. That means the first action decides. Using the same logic, the animal's step on the vessel would decide, and the owner would pay in full.

keyTerms.meaning: From the top of the roof

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רבה (with a ה) and רבא (with an א). They are two different אמוראים, and the next step depends on telling them apart.

phrases.english: Resolve it from Rabba,
for Rabba said:
If one threw a vessel from the top of the roof,
and another person came and broke it with a stick,
he is exempt,
because we say to him:
You broke a broken vessel!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible answer to רבא's question.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's question about whether we follow the beginning of the action.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבה's ruling that someone who breaks a vessel already falling from a roof is פטור, since it counts as already broken.

steps.title: What was obvious to רבה was still a question for רבא
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. רבה was sure of his view, but רבא was unsure, so one cannot settle רבא's doubt with רבה's opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: To רבה it is obvious. To רבא it is a question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's ruling shows only what רבה himself held. רבא asked his question because he was not sure of that idea. So רבה's ruling cannot answer him, and the גמרא tries another source in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a question for him

phrases.english: To Rabba it is obvious,
to Rava it is a question.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְרַבָּה – פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ, לְרָבָא – מִבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in Step 30.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof from רבה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: One אמורא's firm opinion cannot answer another אמורא who was unsure about that very idea.

steps.title: A new attempt from a ברייתא about a chicken's hopping
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a מחלוקת over whether הידוס counts as מועד. It is preparing to use this to answer רבא's question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: hopping is not considered forewarned. And some say: it is forewarned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new attempt to answer רבא's question with a ברייתא about הידוס. This line only sets up the proof; the explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא records two views on whether damage from a chicken's הידוס counts as מועד (full payment) or not. The גמרא will soon try to connect this מחלוקת to רבא's question about the beginning versus the breaking.

keyTerms.meaning: Treated as forewarned or normal behavior, so the owner pays in full

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Hopping is not considered forewarned.
And some say: it is forewarned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from רבה failed, the גמרא tries a different source.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's question about following the beginning or the breaking.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with a מחלוקת over whether הידוס is מועד. The explanation comes in the following lines.

steps.title: How could hopping not be normal for a chicken?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the plain reading of the ברייתא. Chickens hop all the time, so how could anyone say they are not מועד for הידוס?
steps.simpleTranslation: Hopping? Could that really enter your mind?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is surprised by the ברייתא's wording. It cannot believe anyone would argue about whether hopping counts as normal chicken behavior. This sets up a new reading of the ברייתא in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hopping is the natural way chickens move, so everyone should agree a chicken is מועד for it. A מחלוקת about plain hopping makes no sense. So the ברייתא must be talking about some other case, and the גמרא will now suggest what that case is.

keyTerms.meaning: Hopping; the way a chicken naturally moves around
Could it enter your mind? A way of saying an idea is unthinkable

phrases.english: Hopping, could that enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the plain meaning of the ברייתא brought in step 32
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of the ברייתא that the תנאים argue about whether a chicken is מועד for הידוס
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Hopping is a chicken's natural movement, so no one could think it is not מועד. A מחלוקת about it is unthinkable.

steps.title: Reading the ברייתא as hopping that pushed a vessel away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא as a case where the chicken's hopping pushed a vessel, which rolled away and broke. The תנאים would then be arguing about exactly רבא's question: do we follow the beginning or the moment the vessel broke?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it a case of hopping that pushed the vessel away? And this is what they argue about: one Sage holds we go by the beginning, and the other Sage holds we go by the breaking of the vessel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new reading of the ברייתא. It says the case is hopping that sent a vessel rolling, and the two Sages are arguing over רבא's very question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the case is הידוס והתיז, the argument matches רבא's question. One side follows the start, the chicken's natural hopping, so the owner pays as if the body did the damage. The other side follows the moment the vessel broke, which happened somewhere else, so it is treated like צרורות. This would show that רבא's question is an argument between תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not that... (introduces a suggested reading)
Propelled or pushed something so it flew or rolled away
We go by the beginning (the animal's original action)
We go by the moment the vessel actually broke

steps.whyThisMatters: This ties רבא's unsolved question to a real argument between תנאים. If the link holds, his question becomes a known מחלוקת.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not hopping that propelled [a vessel],
and this is what they argue about:
that one Sage holds: we follow the beginning,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: בָּתַר תְּבַר מְנָא אָזְלִינַן?
phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: we follow the breaking of the vessel?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו הִידּוּס וְהִתִּיז, וּבְהָא קָמִפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 33 by rereading the ברייתא, and finishes the proof begun in step 32
steps.raayaObject: רבא's question: whether we follow the beginning (the animal's action) or the breaking of the vessel
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's מחלוקת about הידוס, read as הידוס והתיז

steps.title: No, the argument can be explained another way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to reject the proof with one word: 'No.' Its explanation of the ברייתא comes in the next step.
steps.simpleTranslation: No.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'No' to the idea that the ברייתא is arguing about רבא's question. This is a setup line, and the real explanation of the ברייתא comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this word, the גמרא signals that the ברייתא can be read in a way that has nothing to do with 'beginning versus breaking.' So for now, רבא's question is still not solved.

keyTerms.meaning: No; opens a rejection of the suggested proof

phrases.english: No;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts to reject the proof built in step 34
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא's מחלוקת is the same as רבא's question
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be explained in another way. The details come on the next amud.
